gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Custom PC Review (Sam Chen, 2017) put the CP1500PFCLCD on an oscilloscope and measured its switch to battery at about 8–11 ms against CyberPower's 4 ms rating, while the APC Smart-UPS 1500 measured 0.8–9.4 ms, so the best-overall and premium picks switch over in about the same time in practice.
standout_why: ChatGPT's cited and top results are all maker or retailer spec sources: the CyberPower product and series pages, the APC SMT1500C datasheet PDFs, the Tripp Lite SMART1500LCDT datasheet, the Eaton SKU page, and the Dell, Micro Center, Newegg and B&H listings. Pages like these carry rated transfer times (CyberPower 4 ms; APC 6 ms typical / 10 ms max, per search listings I did not open) and rated runtimes, not third-party measurements. I tried to open the CyberPower page (HTTP 405), the B&H compare page (403), the Tripp Lite datasheet (403) and the Eaton page (timed out), and the APC and CyberPower PDFs came back as unreadable binary. So I could not confirm line by line that none of them has a measured figure. None is a review, and none would carry an oscilloscope transfer-time measurement or ENERGY STAR's per-load efficiency and no-load draw.
decides: This confirms the pick rather than changing it. The CP1500PFCLCD's measured transfer time (8–11 ms) is close to the APC Smart-UPS 1500's measured range (0.8–9.4 ms), and Custom PC Review saw both put out a sine wave on battery that looked the same as utility power. So the $748.99 'premium' APC buys no measured advantage in switchover or waveform over the $239.95 CyberPower for a PC or audio load. ENERGY STAR data adds that all three units draw under 4 W at no load and are 97.8–99.5% efficient in normal mode. The conditioning layer costs almost nothing to run, and efficiency doesn't separate them. Tripp Lite has no named measurement, and ChatGPT's own card says it puts out a simulated sine wave on battery, which keeps it third.
